patterns.rewrite: Do not use food that has spoiled — gone slimy, moldy, decayed or off-smelling. Discard it, and plan to buy less next time. When in doubt, throw it out.

citation.title: Are You Storing Food Safely?
citation.quote: Be aware that food can make you very sick even when it doesn't look, smell, or taste spoiled. That's because foodborne illnesses are caused by pathogenic bacteria, which are different from the spoilage bacteria that make foods "go bad."

patterns.rewrite: Leafy greens that are slimy, mushy or too far gone go in the bin — spoilage cannot be washed, trimmed or cooked away. Use greens within their quality window (spinach keeps 3–7 days refrigerated) and freeze what you cannot use in time. When in doubt, throw it out.

citation.title: Are You Storing Food Safely?
citation.quote: Be alert for spoiled food. Anything that looks or smells suspicious should be thrown out.

patterns.rewrite: Discard produce that is rotten, decaying or has sprouted — cooking does not make spoiled produce safe. Use produce before its quality window instead. When in doubt, throw it out.

citation.title: Selecting and Serving Produce Safely
citation.quote: Cut away any damaged or bruised areas on fresh fruits and vegetables before preparing and/or eating. Throw away any produce that looks rotten.

patterns.rewrite: Raw fish is not made safe by curing, marinating or citrus juice. Use fish that was previously frozen — freezing kills parasites — or cook it to 63 °C (145 °F) on a food thermometer.

citation.title: Fresh and Frozen Seafood: Selecting and Serving It Safely
citation.quote: It's always best to cook seafood thoroughly to minimize the risk of foodborne illness. However, if you choose to eat raw fish anyway, one rule of thumb is to eat fish that has been previously frozen. Some species of fish can contain parasites, and freezing will kill any parasites that may be present. However, be aware that freezing doesn't kill all harmful germs. That's why the safest route is to cook your seafood.

patterns.rewrite: Smell is not a safety test: bacteria that cause food poisoning do not change how food smells or looks. Judge by time and temperature instead — the 2-hour rule and the storage window — and discard what has passed them. When in doubt, throw it out.

citation.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
citation.title: Refrigeration and Food Safety
citation.quote: Pathogenic bacteria can grow rapidly in the "Danger Zone," the temperature range between 40 and 140 °F, but they do not generally affect the taste, smell, or appearance of a food. In other words, one cannot tell that a pathogen is present.
